title: Corpus Linguistics for Teachers

points.sub: A large, searchable sample of real language
pts: A corpus is a large, structured collection of authentic language, searchable for patterns of actual use.
General corpora (like the British National Corpus) sample broad language use; specialised corpora focus on a genre, register or context.
This gives teachers direct evidence of usage, rather than relying on intuition or a coursebook's simplified account.

v: A phone or computer with internet access; one free corpus interface

items: Choose a word you teach this week, for example advice or research.
Search for it in a general corpus interface and note the total frequency.
Look at the first 20 lines of results and note what surprises you.
Compare its frequency with a related word (advice and suggestion, research and study).
Decide whether the comparison changes how much time you will give each word.
In a DIET session, each group searches a different textbook word and reports back.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: What a teacher might notice with research:

lines: It is used mostly as an uncountable noun: do research, carry out research, a lot of research.
The plural researches is rare in general British and American corpora.
It often appears in academic and news writing, much less in conversation.

blocks.x: The corpus does not give a rule; it gives evidence of use, from which the teacher decides what to teach (Hunston 2002).

body: Purpose: to explain a corpus simply. Content: a large library of texts (newspapers, novels, conversations, lectures) feeding into a single search box, with a list of results coming out. Style: clean, friendly. Board version: many small rectangles feeding into one search box.

items: English-Corpora.org (free with registration; daily query limits) for the BNC and COCA [VERIFY current access terms].
SkELL (Sketch Engine for Language Learning; free, no registration).

blocks.x: Two or three learner dictionaries compared for the examples they give; many are corpus-based.

points.sub: Seeing a word in its natural habitat
pts: A concordance search shows every instance of a word or phrase in context across the corpus, line by line.
This reveals typical collocations, grammatical patterns and register associations far more concretely than a dictionary definition.
This directly extends Unit 5's frequency principle into a hands-on, evidence-based teaching tool.

v: A printed set of 15–20 concordance lines for one word

items: Explain the format: each line shows the search word in the centre, with context on either side.
Learners read the lines and circle the word immediately before and after the search word.
In pairs, they list the patterns they see and count each.
They write a ‘rule of use’ in their own words.
Check against a learner dictionary and discuss any differences.
For B1, use shorter lines and ask one focused question, such as ‘Which preposition follows this word?’
Support: highlight the search word and one neighbouring word in each line.
Challenge: learners sort the lines by the word to the right and to the left.

blocks.x: Concordance-style lines for depend (written for this book to show the format):

lines: …the price will | depend | on the size of the order…
…whether we go | depends | on the weather…
…Many families | depend | on the income from…
…It all | depends | .

blocks.x: Learners’ rule: depend is almost always followed by on (or upon), or stands alone in It depends. Working out patterns from the data is Johns’s (1991) data-driven learning.

body: Purpose: to show how a concordance display works. Content: a stack of text lines, each with the same word lined up in a highlighted central column, and arrows pointing to the words on either side. Style: technical but clear. Board version: five lines written with the keyword underlined and aligned.

items: SkELL (free) for short, clean example sentences.
Compleat Lexical Tutor (free) for concordances from several corpora.

blocks.x: Printed concordance lines, prepared once and kept in a file; or sentences collected from newspapers by learners.

pts: A quick concordance check can confirm or challenge a coursebook's simplified grammar rule or usage claim.
This connects directly to Unit 13's coursebook-audit principle, now with a concrete, fast verification method attached.
Building this into routine lesson preparation catches oversimplification before it reaches the classroom.

items: While preparing a lesson, note any rule or usage claim you are unsure of.
Search the key word or structure in a corpus.
Scan 30–50 lines and ask: does the evidence support the coursebook’s claim?
If it does not, decide whether to adjust the explanation, add a note, or simply avoid overstating the rule.
Record the finding in a ‘corpus notes’ page for future years.
Share one check a week at a cluster meeting.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A familiar coursebook rule: ‘Use some in positive sentences and any in questions and negatives.’

lines: A corpus check quickly shows some in offers and requests: Would you like some tea? Could I have some water?
It also shows any in positive sentences meaning ‘it doesn’t matter which’: Any student can join the club.

blocks.x: The rule is a useful starting point, but it is too simple. The teacher adds a note about offers and requests, rather than telling learners that some in questions is wrong. This is the coursebook audit of Unit 13 with a concrete method attached.

body: Purpose: to show verifying a rule against data. Content: a coursebook page with a rule in a box, and a magnifying glass over a set of corpus lines beside it; two lines are ticked, one is flagged. Style: clean. Board version: a rule written on one side and example lines on the other.

items: English-Corpora.org (free with registration; limits) or SkELL (free).

blocks.x: Check two learner dictionaries and a reference grammar before the lesson.

body: Choose one genuinely uncertain question per week rather than trying to check everything. A small, regular habit builds a reliable personal ‘corpus notes’ file within a term.

pts: Collocation is which words typically co-occur; colligation is which grammatical patterns a word typically appears in.
Corpus data reveals both far more reliably than native-speaker intuition alone, which is often patchy for less common items.
This connects directly to Unit 5's lexical-chunk teaching, now grounded in concrete frequency evidence.

v: Collocation data for three words printed as lists

items: Explain two terms: collocation (words that often occur together, such as heavy rain) and colligation (the grammatical patterns a word prefers, such as suggest + -ing or suggest that…).
Give groups the most frequent collocates of three near-synonyms, for example big, large and great.
Groups identify which nouns each adjective prefers and suggest why.
Give a second list showing the grammatical patterns of suggest and recommend.
Learners write five sentences using the patterns and check them with a partner.
Focus on verb–noun collocations: make a decision, take a photo, give a speech.
Support: give each group only one word and five collocates.
Challenge: learners search the corpus themselves and present one surprising collocation.

lines: T: We say strong tea but not powerful tea, even though the meanings are close.
S: So how do we learn them?
T: By noticing them in reading, recording them as chunks, and checking when you are unsure.
She suggested going by train. / She suggested that we go by train.
Much rarer in native-speaker corpora: She suggested us to go.

blocks.x: The strong tea example is Halliday’s classic illustration of collocation. Corpus evidence makes such patterns visible (Sinclair 1991; Hoey 2005).

body: Purpose: to show collocation and colligation. Content: a word at the centre of a circle of ‘friends’ (its collocates), and below it a set of grammatical ‘paths’ (its patterns). Style: friendly, diagrammatic. Board version: a word in the centre with lines to five collocates.

items: SkELL (free) word sketches showing collocates by grammatical relation.
Sketch Engine (subscription; free trial available) for fuller word sketches.
Just the Word (free) for quick collocation checks [VERIFY current availability].

blocks.x: A collocation dictionary, such as the Oxford Collocations Dictionary for Students of English, shared by the department.

pts: Corpora tagged for register reveal how usage shifts between spoken and written, formal and informal contexts.
This gives Unit 27's sociolinguistic competence work concrete, evidence-based material to draw on.
A word or structure common in one register may be rare or absent in another — corpus data makes this visible directly.

v: Frequency information by register for six words or structures

items: Give learners six items: for example get, moreover, kind of, thus, you know, and the passive voice.
Learners predict whether each is more typical of conversation or of academic writing.
Show frequency information by register from a corpus or a corpus-based grammar.
Groups discuss the surprises and what they mean for their own speaking and writing.
Learners rewrite a short, informal paragraph in an academic register.
Compare English usage with register differences in learners’ home languages, such as formal and colloquial Tamil.
Support: work with three items and a simple ‘more in speech / more in writing’ chart.
Challenge: learners find a pair of near-synonyms that differ mainly in register.

blocks.x: General patterns reported in corpus-based grammars (Biber et al. 1999):

lines: get is far more frequent in conversation than in academic prose.
Linking adverbials such as thus and moreover are much more typical of academic writing than of conversation.
The passive is much more common in academic writing than in conversation.

blocks.x: A learner who writes Moreover, my friend and I went to the cinema in a chatty email has used a correct word in the wrong register. This gives the sociolinguistic competence of Unit 27 an evidence base.

body: Purpose: to show register variation. Content: a split scene: on one side friends chatting at a tea stall, on the other a student writing an essay; word bubbles show which words appear in each, with size showing frequency. Style: warm, clear. Board version: two columns headed ‘chat’ and ‘essay’ with words in different sizes.

items: English-Corpora.org (free with registration) for frequency by genre in COCA.

blocks.x: Printed frequency charts from a corpus-based grammar or teacher’s book.

pts: Use concordance lines directly, lightly edited, as authentic example sentences for teaching materials.
This is often faster and more reliable than inventing example sentences from scratch, and avoids unintentionally unnatural phrasing.
This connects to Unit 41's authentic-materials-at-scale principle, applied at the sentence and phrase level.

v: A corpus tool; a materials template

items: Choose a target structure or phrase for a worksheet.
Search for it and collect 20 lines.
Select five or six lines that are clear, typical and suitable for your learners.
Edit lightly: shorten, remove rare names or offensive content, but keep the pattern and natural phrasing.
Record the source of each example.
Collect examples from ICE-India or other Indian English sources alongside British and American ones.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Invented versus corpus-sourced example, for used to:

lines: Invented: I used to go to school by the bus every day in my childhood days.
Corpus-style, lightly edited: We used to walk to school, about three kilometres each way.

blocks.x: The invented example contains a small unnatural phrase (by the bus). Real examples help avoid such slips. Record sources and keep edits light; the aim is authentic phrasing, as in the authentic materials work of Unit 41.

body: Purpose: to show examples being selected and edited. Content: a concordance printout with some lines ticked, an arrow to a neat worksheet where those lines appear as numbered examples. Style: tidy, practical. Board version: a list with ticks and an arrow to a numbered list.

items: SkELL (free) for short example sentences ready for editing.
Google Docs (free) for keeping a bank of sourced examples.

blocks.x: Examples collected from newspapers and graded readers, with the source noted.

pts: A learner corpus — a collection of learner writing or speech — reveals patterns of error and interlanguage across a whole cohort.
This connects directly to Unit 49's error-analysis-as-diagnosis principle, now conducted with systematic corpus tools rather than informal observation.
Comparing a learner corpus against a native-speaker reference corpus highlights genuinely distinctive interlanguage patterns.

v: Typed learner writing (with consent); a free concordancer

items: Collect one piece of writing from each learner on the same task, typed and anonymized.
Save them as plain-text files in one folder.
Load them into a free concordancer and search for items you suspect are problems.
Compare with a reference corpus to see which patterns are distinctive.
Use the findings to plan focused language work for the class (Unit 49).
Build a school corpus over several years, so that trends across cohorts become visible.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Findings from one class set of 45 essays (a fictional class):

lines: discuss about appears in 11 essays; in a British reference corpus, discuss almost always takes a direct object.
In today’s world opens 19 essays: not an error, but an overused formula.
Only 3 essays use however in the middle of a sentence.

blocks.x: A learner corpus turns scattered impressions into cohort-level evidence (Granger 1998). The teacher can see which patterns affect most of the class, and plan accordingly.

body: Purpose: to show a learner corpus revealing shared patterns. Content: a pile of essays fed into a laptop, producing a short bar chart of the most frequent learner patterns. Style: clean. Board version: a pile of pages, an arrow, a bar chart.

items: AntConc (free) desktop concordancer for small, homemade corpora.

blocks.x: A tally sheet: read 20 scripts and tally five target features by hand.

pts: Free, accessible corpus tools exist for general and academic English, requiring no specialist technical background to begin using.
Start with a single genuinely uncertain usage question in lesson preparation, rather than attempting comprehensive corpus analysis from day one.
This connects to Unit 18's digital-tools principle — the tool should serve a specific, real teaching need, not be adopted for its own sake.

v: 15 minutes a week for four weeks

items: Each week, write down one real usage question that arose in class or during preparation.
Choose the tool that best fits the question: concordance, collocation, frequency or register.
Spend no more than ten minutes finding an answer.
Record what you found and how you used it.
After four weeks, review: which questions were easiest to answer, and which tool served you best?
Run the task as a teacher circle, with each member sharing one question a week.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A four-week log (written for this book):

lines: Week 1: Is ‘prepone’ used outside India? → rare in British and American corpora; common in Indian English. Told learners it may not be understood abroad.
Week 2: Which verb goes with ‘progress’? → make progress.
Week 3: Is ‘whilst’ formal? → more common in British writing; less in American. Accept both.
Week 4: What follows ‘look forward to’? → -ing or a noun.

blocks.x: The tool serves a specific teaching need, not the other way round, as Unit 18 argued for all digital tools.

body: Purpose: to encourage a small, regular habit. Content: a teacher’s notebook with four dated entries, each a short question with a small magnifying-glass icon and a one-line answer. Style: warm, handwritten. Board version: four lines in a list.

items: SkELL, English-Corpora.org and AntConc (all free) as a starter set.

blocks.x: A learner dictionary and a reference grammar, used with the same one-question habit.

body: For the next four weeks, keep a corpus log. Answer one real usage question a week in under ten minutes, and use the answer in a lesson. At the end, share your two most useful findings with a colleague.

dek: Unit 58 of 100: building genuine, practical skill with corpus tools — replacing intuition and coursebook simplification with real evidence of how language is actually used.

aims.x: Every teacher has been asked a question they could not answer with confidence: ‘Can we say discuss about?’, ‘Is moreover used in speaking?’, ‘Why is it heavy rain but not heavy sun?’ Intuition helps, but it is patchy, especially for less common words and for varieties of English we do not use ourselves. A corpus lets us look at the evidence. This unit builds the occasional corpus check mentioned in Unit 13 into a practical, regular skill for lesson preparation, materials writing and feedback.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what a corpus is, and distinguish general, specialized and learner corpora;
run a concordance search and read concordance lines for patterns;
check a coursebook rule or usage claim against corpus evidence in a few minutes;
identify the collocations and colligations of a word;
compare how usage varies across spoken and written, formal and informal registers;
select and lightly edit concordance lines as example sentences for materials;
use a learner corpus for cohort-level error analysis, and choose free tools suited to a specific teaching question.

why: Why this matters. Unit 13 mentioned checking corpus evidence occasionally. This poster builds that occasional check into a genuine, regularly-used analytical skill.

background.x: A corpus (plural corpora) is a large, principled collection of real texts, spoken and written, stored electronically so that it can be searched. The British National Corpus, compiled in the 1990s, contains about 100 million words of British English from many sources (Hunston 2002). John Sinclair, who led the COBUILD project at Birmingham, argued that corpus evidence changes our picture of language: meaning is carried less by single words than by the patterns they habitually form with other words (Sinclair 1991). Michael Hoey’s (2005) theory of lexical priming develops this idea. For teachers, the practical result is the lexical approach to vocabulary described in Unit 5, and the emphasis on chunks, collocations and frequency.

Corpus research has already changed teaching materials. Learner dictionaries and grammars now draw on corpus evidence, and the Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English (Biber et al. 1999) showed in detail how grammar differs between conversation, fiction, news and academic prose. Anne O’Keeffe, Michael McCarthy and Ronald Carter (2007) set out what corpus findings mean for the classroom, including the special grammar of spoken English. Tim Johns (1991) proposed data-driven learning, in which learners themselves examine concordance lines and work out patterns, acting as researchers. A meta-analysis by Alex Boulton and Tom Cobb (2017) found generally positive effects of such corpus use on learning, though the studies varied widely.

Corpora are also relevant to Indian English and to multilingual classrooms. The Kolhapur Corpus of Indian English and the India component of the International Corpus of English (ICE-India) make it possible to compare Indian usage with British or American usage on the evidence, not on prejudice. That comparison matters for Unit 59 and Unit 74: some features that teachers mark as errors are established features of Indian English, while others are genuinely learner forms. Learner corpora, such as the International Corpus of Learner English (Granger 1998), show what learners with particular first languages tend to produce. NCF 2023 encourages teachers to use evidence and to adapt materials thoughtfully (NCERT 2023). A few minutes with a free corpus tool is one simple way to do that.

items: Coursebook check. A short report on one coursebook rule checked against corpus evidence, with a proposed classroom note.
Collocation materials. A worksheet built from lightly edited concordance lines, with sources recorded.
Learner corpus mini-study. An analysis of five target features in one class set of writing, with a plan for teaching.
Corpus log. Four weekly entries showing questions, tools used, findings and classroom use.
Which usage questions from learners have you found hardest to answer confidently?
How often does your coursebook simplify a rule in a way that might mislead learners?
How do you decide whether a form is an Indian English feature or a learner error?
Where would corpus evidence most improve your own materials?
What would a small corpus of your learners’ writing tell you that marking alone does not?

perm: All concordance-style lines, logs and examples are written for this book to illustrate format and do not reproduce any corpus output. Real concordance lines used in published materials must follow the terms of the corpus interface. Screenshots of SkELL, Sketch Engine, English-Corpora.org, Compleat Lexical Tutor or AntConc require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Learner writing used in a class corpus requires consent and anonymization.

terms.def: The grammatical patterns a word tends to occur with, such as suggest followed by -ing or a that-clause; related to collocation, which concerns word partnerships.
A combination of words that frequently occur together, such as make a decision or heavy rain; learners who know collocations sound more natural and fluent.
A list of all the examples of a word or phrase in a corpus, shown with their context and aligned on the key word, used to study patterns of use.
A large, principled collection of real spoken or written texts stored electronically, used to study how language is actually used; plural corpora.
An approach in which learners examine concordance lines from a corpus and work out patterns for themselves, acting as researchers (Johns 1991).
How often a word, phrase or structure occurs in a corpus of real language. It helps teachers decide which items to teach first and how much time to give them.

A principled electronic collection of texts produced by learners of a language, used to identify common errors and patterns at a given level; a teacher can compile one from a cohort’s essays for error analysis.

The theory that each word becomes associated, through repeated encounters, with the words, grammar and contexts it typically occurs with, so that speakers expect and reproduce these patterns (Hoey 2005).

A large, general collection of texts used as a benchmark against which a smaller corpus, such as learners’ essays, is compared to show which patterns are distinctive or unusual, for example learners’ frequent ‘discuss about’.

Variation in language according to the situation of use, especially the subject matter, the relationship between participants and the channel of communication. A learner writes differently in a WhatsApp message to a friend and a leave letter to the headteacher.
